Although we have docs#Submodule.FG, we mostly use docs#Module.Finite (or docs#FiniteDimensional) to express that a subtype is finite dimensional. This is frequently quite painful, especially when we want to use simp. For example, the following fails:

import Mathlib

example {R M : Type*} [Ring R] [TopologicalSpace M] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
    {A B : Submodule R M} (eq : A = B) :
    Module.Finite R A ↔ Module.Finite R B := by
  simp [eq] -- fails
  sorry

On the other hand, this would work perfectly fine with Submodule.FG. Does this suggest we should use the latter more (and potentially make it a class) ? Note that the same issue occurs with docs#Module.rank, docs#Module.finrank, etc... Also, I can't find it again, but the recent rigidity with transparency makes it worse in some cases.
I know it does! I remember finding examples where even rw fails without a set_option, but I can't reconstruct them. But simp failing is bad enough I claim.

If we really want to have a single user-facing definition, maybe we could have a simproc for simplifying this kind of things ? As in, simplifying the expression for the submodule, then using docs#LinearEquiv.ofEq to conclude equality of dimension ? This is very naive.

I have always been scared by these kinds of arguments. We have A = B but surely typeclass inference will still struggle to show that the AddCommGroup structure on ↥A and ↥B are "equal" because the equality is not syntactic.
Yes, I agree this is morally bad, and we've been abusing it for too long! But if we used docs#Submodule.FG then there'd be no problem at all.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I have always been scared by these kinds of arguments. We have A = B but surely typeclass inference will still struggle to show that the AddCommGroup structure on ↥A and ↥B are "equal" because the equality is not syntactic.

The instances in the goal here are Submodule.addCommMonoid A and Submodule.addCommMonoid B, so it's easy enough to see that they're "equal". But I can imagine in more complicated cases this would be more difficult (for example, if there's an instance that applies to A but not to B).

(I've had a bad example of this happening to me today: I had a submodule A whose simp normal form was A' (which happened to be def-eq to A), and simp simplified the goal by replacing A by A', but the instances kept mentioning A.)
I absolutely agree with Anatole. This is also why I have been wanting Submodule.finrank (which doesn't exist yet)
We have all this API for subspaces of topological spaces and it seems to work well for us so why not?
